power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Low haemoglobin concentration, or anaemia, is a major global public health issue, particularly severe in sub-Saharan Africa, including East Africa, where prevalence rates are alarmingly high.
This situation requires a comprehensive analysis to identify the key factors contributing to this high prevalence, especially in East Africa.
This study uses robust quantile regression to examine the relationship between maternal haemoglobin concentration and child haemoglobin levels in three East African countries.
The study analysed data from the Demographic and Health Surveys of three East African countries: Ethiopia, Tanzania, and Uganda.
These data are nationally representative and are collected every five years from low-and middleincome countries.
The analysis included a total sample of 6,883 children and their mothers.
The primary outcome variable was the child's haemoglobin concentration.
We used quantile regression to model the effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration on child haemoglobin levels, adjusting for potential confounders.

Results: The results showed that a one-unit increase in maternal haemoglobin (Hb) concentration was associated with a unit increase in child haemoglobin concentration as follows: In Tanzania, the increases were 0.19, 0.20, 0.19, and 0.17 at the 5th, 10th, 25th, and 50th quantiles, respectively.
In Ethiopia, the increases were 0.23, 0.22, 0.22, and 0.17 at the same quantiles.
In Uganda, the increases were 0.19, 0.19, 0.18, and 0.19 at these quantiles.

In contrast, a one-unit increase in maternal Hb concentration was associated with a smaller increase in child Hb concentration, ranging from 0.11 to 0.13 at the upper quantiles (75th and 90th) across all three countries.
Overall, the most significant effects of maternal Hb . concentration on child Hb levels were observed at the lower end of the conditional Hb distribution in each of the three countries.
Conclusion: Maternal haemoglobin (Hb) concentration is positively associated with children's haemoglobin levels across all countries studied.
The strongest association is among children in the lower quantiles, who are at higher risk of anaemia.
In contrast, the association is less pronounced among those in the upper quantiles.
Therefore, improving maternal Hb is likely to benefit children in the lower quantiles more than those in the upper quantiles.
Programmes aimed at addressing child anaemia should consider these differing effects of maternal Hb concentration.
Childhood anaemia, commonly known as low haemoglobin (Hb) concentration, reflects a reduced red blood cell count or diminished oxygen-carrying capacity (1).
text.formatted: Childhood anaemia, commonly known as low haemoglobin (Hb) concentration, reflects a reduced red blood cell count or diminished oxygen-carrying capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: This condition is a major public health problem, affecting an estimated 40% of children aged 6 to 59 months worldwide (1).
text.formatted: This condition is a major public health problem, affecting an estimated 40% of children aged 6 to 59 months worldwide <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: The situation is particularly severe in sub-Saharan Africa, where the prevalence is estimated at 64%, and in some countries, it exceeds 80% (2, 3).
text.formatted: The situation is particularly severe in sub-Saharan Africa, where the prevalence is estimated at 64%, and in some countries, it exceeds 80% <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">3)</ref>.

text.text: In East Africa, the average prevalence is 55.6% (4).
In some specific East African countries, such as Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda, the burden is 56%, 52%, and 52%, respectively (5).
text.formatted: In some specific East African countries, such as Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda, the burden is 56%, 52%, and 52%, respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref>.

text.text: This substantial prevalence underscores the urgent need to identify the primary determinants of childhood anaemia in the region, so that effective interventions can be designed and targeted appropriately.
Low Hb concentration can have significant short-and long-term effects on children's health.

Anaemia negatively affects various aspects of a child's wellbeing, including developmental delays, impaired cognitive development (which can reduce learning ability and school performance), weakened immunity, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, lethargy, increased mortality, and heightened susceptibility to infections (1).
text.formatted: Anaemia negatively affects various aspects of a child's wellbeing, including developmental delays, impaired cognitive development (which can reduce learning ability and school performance), weakened immunity, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, lethargy, increased mortality, and heightened susceptibility to infections <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, childhood anaemia is linked to a reduced ability to fight infections, contributing to morbidity and mortality among children (1).
text.formatted: Moreover, childhood anaemia is linked to a reduced ability to fight infections, contributing to morbidity and mortality among children <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref>.

text.text: The extant literature suggests that various factors, including deficiencies in essential nutrients such as iron, folate, vitamin B12, and copper, influence low haemoglobin levels in children.

Other contributing elements include insufficient dietary intake, poor nutrient absorption, and increased physiological needs during periods of rapid growth, along with key sociodemographic factors at the maternal and household levels (7).
text.formatted: Other contributing elements include insufficient dietary intake, poor nutrient absorption, and increased physiological needs during periods of rapid growth, along with key sociodemographic factors at the maternal and household levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: However, this study focuses on the effects of maternal haemoglobin concentration on their children's haemoglobin levels.
This focus is justified by evidence of a strong relationship between maternal and child haemoglobin concentrations (7, 8).
text.formatted: This focus is justified by evidence of a strong relationship between maternal and child haemoglobin concentrations <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8)</ref>.

text.text: Several studies have also documented a strong association between maternal haemoglobin concentration and childhood anaemia (low haemoglobin concentration) (3, (7) (8) (9) (10) (11) (12).
text.formatted: Several studies have also documented a strong association between maternal haemoglobin concentration and childhood anaemia (low haemoglobin concentration) <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(10)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(12)</ref>.

text.text: Compared to children of non-anaemic mothers, children of anaemic mothers are approximately 13.5% more likely to be anaemic themselves (9).
text.formatted: Compared to children of non-anaemic mothers, children of anaemic mothers are approximately 13.5% more likely to be anaemic themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: A cross-sectional study conducted in rural Zimbabwe found a significant link between maternal anaemia and anaemia in children aged 6 to 59 months, indicating a crossgenerational relationship (8).
text.formatted: A cross-sectional study conducted in rural Zimbabwe found a significant link between maternal anaemia and anaemia in children aged 6 to 59 months, indicating a crossgenerational relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: The research emphasised that improving maternal nutritional status is essential for reducing the high rates of child anaemia in lowincome settings (8).
text.formatted: The research emphasised that improving maternal nutritional status is essential for reducing the high rates of child anaemia in lowincome settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref>.

text.text: This intergenerational connection largely stems from shared nutritional deficiencies, socioeconomic factors, and infections, which often lower haemoglobin levels (9).
text.formatted: This intergenerational connection largely stems from shared nutritional deficiencies, socioeconomic factors, and infections, which often lower haemoglobin levels <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(9)</ref>.

text.text: Many other studies have identified maternal anaemia as a key driver of child haemoglobin concentration levels.

In a study using data from 47 Sub-Saharan African (SSA) countries, researchers found that the highest anaemia prevalence occurred in children whose mothers were moderately or severely anaemic, at 76.8% and 76.7%, respectively (3).
This indicates that children of anaemic mothers are more likely to experience higher levels of anaemia compared to children whose mothers are not anaemic.
The existing literature on the relationship between maternal and child anaemia levels abounds.
However, the analytical methods used in previous studies have significant limitations.
Most of these studies have relied on Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) or logistic regression to estimate the effects of maternal Hb concentration on child Hb levels.
These approaches may overlook the varying effects that maternal Hb concentration can have on child Hb levels.
This variability highlights the need for a more comprehensive analysis to understand how maternal Hb concentration influences child Hb status across the Hb concentration distribution.
Therefore, this study employs quantile regression, a method that allows for the examination of maternal Hb effects at various points within the conditional distribution of child Hb concentration.
Such an analysis is currently lacking in the field of child anaemia research.
This analysis utilised the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) data sets (13) from three East African countries: Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda.
text.formatted: This analysis utilised the Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) data sets <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(13)</ref> from three East African countries: Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda.

text.text: We chose these countries because they are the countries in EA which have data on child and maternal Haemoglobin.
The DHS survey design is consistent across these countries, allowing meaningful comparisons.
The DHS employed a two-stage sampling design.
In the first stage, clusters were selected from an updated master sampling frame based on the National Population and Housing Census of each country.
Clusters were chosen using systematic sampling with probability proportional to size.
Following this, household listings were conducted in all selected clusters to create a sampling frame for the second stage.
In the second stage, households from the listed households in each cluster were systematically sampled, with selections made randomly from the list.
This approach ensures an adequate number of completed individual interviews, allowing reliable estimates of key indicators with acceptable precision.

All women aged 15 to 49, along with their children aged 0-59 months, in the selected households were eligible to participate in the surveys as long as they were either usual residents of the household or visitors present in the household on the night before the survey.
This analysis focuses on children aged 6 to 59 months, the eligible age for inclusion in the Hb data collection.
The total sample sizes used in this analysis were 1797, 3486, and 1600 mother-child dyads, representing Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda, respectively.
The DHS study was conducted in accordance with international ethical best practices (14).
Thus, data collectors were trained to respect the rights of individuals participating in the research.
During data collection, participants were informed of their right to decide whether to take part in the study.
They were also told they could abstain or withdraw (e.g., discontinue an interview) at any time without repercussions.
The study's risks and benefits were clearly explained, along with measures taken to mitigate potential risks.
Well-trained investigators conducted the surveys using an approved protocol.

The relevant national Ethical Review Committees in each country, as well as the Institutional Review Board of ICF International in the USA, reviewed and approved the study protocols, including those for biomarker collection.
The DHS research team obtained written informed consent from mothers before the survey, and for children aged 6-59 months, from their parents or guardians.
The team shared biomarker results with participants.
For example, the Hb test results for all children tested in the household were recorded in a malaria and anaemia brochure and given to the parent or responsible adult.
Additionally, an anaemia referral form was given to facilitate immediate treatment at a nearby health facility for children with an Hb level below 7.0 g/dl.
The authors requested and received permission from the DHS programme to use the data.
Because the data were fully anonymous, the authors did not need to seek additional ethical clearance.
The outcome variable was child Hb concentration.
The DHS collected blood specimens from all children aged 6 to 59 months for anaemia testing.
A drop of blood was obtained through a finger prick for older children and a heel prick for those aged 6 to 11 months.
The blood was collected in a microcuvette.
Hb analysis was performed on-site using a portable battery-powered HaemoCue analyser.

The Hb data were categorised as follows: mild anaemia (Hb concentration of 10.0 to 10.9 grams per deciliter (g/dL)), moderate anaemia (Hb concentration of 7.0 to 9.9 g/dL), and severe anaemia (Hb concentration of less than 7.0 g/dL).
In this analysis, Hb concentration was treated as a continuous variable due to the analytical strategy employed.
Primary explanatory variable.
The exposure was maternal Hb concentration (g/dL), a continuous variable.
The DHS collected blood samples from non-pregnant mothers who consented to participate.
Blood was obtained from a finger prick and analysed on-site using a portable HaemoCue analyser.
Covariates: Covariates were selected based on prior literature and organised into four levels.
At the child level, the covariates included sex, age in months, and vitamin A supplementation during the six months preceding the survey.
Vitamin A supplementation was specifically chosen as a covariate because it raises haemoglobin levels and lowers the risk of anaemia by 26% (15).
text.formatted: Vitamin A supplementation was specifically chosen as a covariate because it raises haemoglobin levels and lowers the risk of anaemia by 26% <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(15)</ref>.

text.text: At the maternal level, the covariates were years of education, age, body mass index (BMI), current employment status, breastfeeding status, and antenatal care (ANC) attendance.
Maternal BMI was categorised as follows: underweight (<18.5 kg/m²), normal weight (18.5-24.9 kg/m²), overweight (25.0-29.9 kg/m²), or obese (≥30 kg/m²).
text.formatted: Maternal BMI was categorised as follows: underweight (<18.5 kg/m²), normal weight (18.5-24.9 kg/m²), overweight (25.0-29.9 kg/m²), or obese (≥30 kg/m²).

text.text: We excluded extreme and implausible values before categorisation.
We classified ANC attendance as adequate (four or more visits) or inadequate (fewer than four visits), in line with WHO recommendations in effect during each survey (16).
text.formatted: We classified ANC attendance as adequate (four or more visits) or inadequate (fewer than four visits), in line with WHO recommendations in effect during each survey <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(16)</ref>.

text.text: At the household level, the covariates included the household wealth index, the sex of the household head, household size, the primary decision-maker for large purchases, and the highest education level of the husband or partner.
At the community level, we also considered place of residence (urban or rural).
Analyses were performed in Stata version 17 using the svyset command to account for the complex survey design .

We computed weighted descriptive statistics for the analytic sample in each country, reporting means and standard deviations for continuous variables and weighted proportions for categorical variables.
To assess crude associations, we first ran bivariate OLS regressions for each covariate against child haemoglobin concentration.

We then included all covariates with evidence of association in bivariate analysis or established theoretical relevance in a multivariable, survey-weighted OLS regression, estimated using svy: reg, which provides unbiased coefficient estimates and design-corrected standard errors under the complex sampling scheme.

The multivariable OLS model estimated the mean difference in child haemoglobin concentration associated with a one-unit increase in maternal haemoglobin concentration, holding all other covariates constant.
We assessed potential multicollinearity among covariates using variance inflation factors (VIF).

To test whether the association between maternal and child haemoglobin concentration varied across the conditional distribution of child haemoglobin, we estimated quantile regression (QR) models at the 5th, 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th percentiles.

Unlike OLS, which estimates effects at the conditional mean, QR characterises the relationship at multiple points of the outcome distribution, offering insight into whether the association is stronger among children with low haemoglobin-where the clinical implications are greatest-than among those with higher levels.
The model was specified as: where is the -th conditional quantile of child haemoglobin concentration, is the effect of maternal haemoglobin at quantile , and is the vector of covariates.
We applied sampling weights in all QR models.
We excluded marital status from the final models in all three countries because of limited variability, with over 83% of mothers reporting they were currently married or cohabiting.
All analyses accounted for the complex survey design of the DHS.
We constructed sampling weights by dividing the DHS weight variable (v005) by 1,000,000.

We declared the survey design in Stata using svyset, specifying primary sampling units (v021) and sampling strata (v022), so variance estimates reflected the stratified cluster structure across all descriptive and regression analyses.
Hb concentration among children in the three countries was similar, with Uganda showing a slightly higher average of 10.33 ± 1.79 g/dL.
Women in Ethiopia had the highest Hb concentration (12.54 ± 2.59 g/dL), while women in Tanzania had the lowest (12.10±2.36).
Tables 2-4 present the results of the multivariable QR analysis for Tanzania, Ethiopia, and Uganda.
To facilitate comparison with the QR findings, we have also included OLS estimates in all tables.
The OLS analysis indicated a positive association between maternal haemoglobin (Hb) concentration and their children's
Hb levels across all three countries and quantiles.
Thus, a unit increase in maternal Hb concentration corresponded to a one-unit increase in the child's Hb level.
However, the QR analysis revealed that the effects of maternal Hb concentration on child Hb levels varied across points in the conditional Hb distribution.

In Tanzania, the strongest association between maternal Hb concentration and child Hb levels was observed in the lower four quantiles, while the weakest associations were noted among children in the upper two quantiles.
A similar pattern emerged in analyses of data from Ethiopia and Uganda, where maternal Hb concentration was positively associated with child Hb levels across all quantiles.
Again, the strongest association was found among children in the lower quantiles, and the weakest association among those in the upper two quantiles.

Specifically, a one-unit increase in maternal Hb concentration was associated with the following increases in child Hb concentration: In Tanzania, 0.19, 0.20, 0.19, and 0.17 at the 5th, 10th, 25th, and 50th quantiles, respectively.
In Ethiopia, the increases were 0.23, 0.22, 0.22, and 0.17 at the same quantiles.
In Uganda, the increases were 0.19, 0.19, 0.18, and 0.19 at the respective quantiles.

In contrast, a one-unit increase in maternal Hb concentration was associated with a smaller increase in child Hb concentration, ranging from 0.11 to 0.13 at the upper quantiles (75th and 90th) across all three countries.

Figures 1-3 present the results of the QR analysis conducted in the three countries.

text.text: Consequently, improving mothers' nutritional status is crucial to reducing high rates of child anaemia in low-income settings.
The study has several notable strengths.

One key strength is that both the outcome variable (child Hb) and the candidate predictor variable (maternal Hb) were objectively measured, which helps minimise potential biases associated with subjective measurements.
Using QR allowed assessment of the effects of maternal Hb concentration across the distribution of child Hb levels, providing a more comprehensive understanding of these effects.
Additionally, using nationally representative data allows the results to be generalised to all children in the respective countries.
However, an important limitation of the study is its crosssectional nature, which makes it difficult to establish causality.
Thus, the findings can only be interpreted as associations between the outcome and predictor variables.

The term "effect" in the manuscript refers to a non-causal association, specifically how changes in the coefficient of the explanatory variable correspond to changes in the coefficient of the outcome variable.
Lastly, missing data can often pose a significant challenge in secondary data analysis.
Fortunately, due to the robustness of the DHS data management system, missing data was not an issue in our analysis.

Our analysis clearly demonstrated heterogamous association between maternal Hb concentration and child Hb levels at different points within the Hb distribution across all countries studied.
The strongest association is observed among children at the lower quantiles who are at high risk of anaemia, whereas the effect is less pronounce among children at the higher quantiles.
Therefore, improving maternal Hb is likely to benefit children in the lower quantiles more than those in the upper quantiles.

Interventions and programmes aimed at addressing child anaemia should account for the varying effects of maternal Hb concentration on child Hb concentration across different Hb distribution quantiles.
